evaluation.positioning_hook: A small-town mayoral frontrunner spends election day trying to hide a corpse in his rental car while his campaign manager, a nosy sheriff, and a ruthless rival turn the whole town into a live crime scene.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise is instantly legible and built for broad laughs: a mayoral candidate, a dead body, a trunk, and a day-long spiral of bad decisions. The appeal is strongest for adult comedy audiences and crime-comedy buyers, though the humor is very specific and the language/content narrow the four-quadrant reach.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands immediately in the opening pages with the body in the trunk and the election-day pressure cooker. The script keeps the engine simple and readable throughout: Tom has to survive the day, keep the body hidden, and not blow the election.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Tom is a strong comic lead because he’s earnest, superstitious, and increasingly desperate, while Stuart gives the movie a second comic engine with his panic and delusion. Karen and Freddie are vivid antagonists, but the supporting cast is more functional than deeply surprising.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script commits to a farcical crime spiral inside a civic-election setting, which gives it a distinct lane. The voice is confident and the escalation is playful, though the underlying mechanics are familiar enough that the originality comes more from execution than from premise invention.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The story keeps adding complications cleanly: the trunk won’t close, the sheriff escorts them, the interview goes live, the house gets invaded, and the warehouse showdown escalates. Each beat creates a new problem rather than repeating the last one, which keeps the movie moving.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The election-day crime farce feels fresh because the civic stakes and the criminal stakes are constantly colliding in public. It’s not a reinvention of the genre, but the combination of small-town politics, trunk comedy, and live-news humiliation gives it a memorable hook.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: Chesterville has enough texture to support the story: the campaign posters, the sheriff, the rental car shop, the warehouse, the local news van, and the town gossip all feel connected. Still, the world mainly serves the plot engine rather than generating a deeper social ecosystem.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a clear comic register: broad, profane, escalating, and proudly ridiculous, with a strong small-town absurdist flavor. The tonal identity is consistent from the opening execution to the final fish-hook sting.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: What you see is largely what you get: a fast, comic crime caper with a straightforward moral center. Tom’s grief over Rebecca and the town’s corruption add some emotional and political texture, but the script is built for immediate payoff more than hidden depth.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Tom/Stuart is a strong comic duo, and the Tom/Marilynn/Wendy household gives the movie a second relationship engine with real friction. Karen/Freddie and Tom/Electra add additional playable pairings, so the movie has enough recurring chemistry to keep generating scenes.

lead_characters.name: Tom Justin
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 40s, small-town mayoral candidate, widower, father.
lead_characters.hook: Tom is a decent, tightly wound local politician who wants to win on sincerity and civic trust, then spends election day trapped in a nightmare of his own making. He’s superstitious, image-conscious, and increasingly feral as the body-in-the-trunk problem collides with his public life, his family life, and his need to look like the town’s moral center.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Steve Carell in The Big Short or Jason Bateman in Arrested Development when the comedy comes from panic under pressure: a man trying to keep dignity while everything around him collapses. The role gives an actor escalating physical comedy, fast verbal timing, and a real emotional anchor in the grief and responsibility underneath the chaos.

lead_characters.name: Stuart
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 40s, Tom’s best friend, local office worker / civilian sidekick.
lead_characters.hook: Stuart is the anxious, inhaler-dependent best friend who keeps making the situation worse while believing he’s helping. He’s a coward with flashes of loyalty, a chronic over-explainer, and the movie’s best source of accidental escalation, especially once he starts improvising his way into danger.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets a comic actor do the Jonah Hill in Superbad thing: high-volume panic, wounded loyalty, and a total lack of self-awareness that still feels lovable. It’s a big physical-comedy part with real scene-stealing potential, especially in the gas station and house-invasion sequences.

lead_characters.name: Karen Riley
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 40s, incumbent mayor, politically ambitious, criminally compromised.
lead_characters.hook: Karen is polished in public and ruthless in private, using the election and the warehouse operation as parallel power plays. She’s the movie’s cleanest antagonist because she can smile through civic language while orchestrating murder, blackmail, and cover-up with total confidence.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the Glenn Close in Damages or Laura Linney in Ozark lane: controlled authority with a predatory edge. The part offers sharp reversals, public-private contrast, and a chance to play intelligence as menace.

lead_characters.name: Freddie
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 20s, criminal associate, dim but dangerous.
lead_characters.hook: Freddie is the good-looking idiot who keeps stumbling into violence, flirtation, and bad decisions with equal confidence. He’s funny because he’s so wrong so often, but he’s also a real threat once the gun comes out and the nosebleed turns him into a chaotic pursuer.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a classic comic-villain showcase in the Ryan Reynolds in Waiting / Chris Messina in The Giant Mechanical Man lane: charm, stupidity, and menace in one package. The role gives an actor a lot of room for physical comedy, sexual bravado, and sudden danger.

lead_characters.name: Marilynn
lead_characters.demographics: Female, early 20s, Tom’s daughter, campaign manager.
lead_characters.hook: Marilynn is the smart, exhausted daughter who is effectively running the campaign while also managing the family’s emotional weather. She’s the only person in the house who seems to understand the stakes, and her patience with Tom and Wendy gives the movie a grounded counterweight to the farce.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the Zoey Deutch in Set It Up or Kaitlyn Dever in Booksmart energy: quick, capable, and perpetually one step ahead of the adults. It’s a strong straight-man/comic-reactor part with authority and warmth.

lead_characters.name: Wendy
lead_characters.hook: Wendy is the meddling, observant matriarch who hears everything, notices everything, and still somehow becomes the household’s most effective operator. She’s funny because she’s nosy and blunt, but she also becomes unexpectedly useful when the house is under threat.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is prime character-actress territory in the Frances Sternhagen / June Squibb lane: dry authority, comic timing, and the pleasure of watching an elder character quietly dominate the room. The role gives an actor sharp one-liners and a late-story turn into active protection.

lead_characters.name: Electra Simms
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 30s, local TV reporter, ambitious, media-savvy.
lead_characters.hook: Electra is the overqualified reporter who knows she’s stuck on a small-market assignment and decides to turn the chaos into a career move. She’s sharp, performative, and opportunistic, but she also has enough charm to make Stuart’s crush and the live-interview sequence pop.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the Allison Janney in Drop Dead Gorgeous or Amy Adams in sharp-satire mode: polished, funny, and always aware of the camera. It’s a great showcase for rapid-fire delivery, vanity, and controlled opportunism.

lead_characters.name: Sheriff Cooper
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 50s, local sheriff, friendly authority figure.
lead_characters.hook: Sheriff Cooper is the genial lawman who keeps almost believing the nonsense he’s hearing until the evidence becomes impossible to ignore. He’s a useful comic authority figure because he’s not stupid, just perpetually a beat behind the truth.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets a veteran character actor play deadpan authority with a slow-burn reveal, in the vein of John Goodman in smaller-town ensemble comedy. The part gives an actor dry reactions, procedural presence, and a payoff in the final reveal.

lead_characters.name: Andy
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 40s, local neighbor/friend, earnest and dim.
lead_characters.hook: Andy is the well-meaning local who keeps stumbling into the plot and somehow helping by accident. He’s simple, sincere, and oddly heroic in the final stretch, which makes him a useful comic wildcard rather than just a punchline.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the Paul Rudd-in-supporting-comedy lane: affable, confused, and unexpectedly essential. The part has a late-game hero beat that can land big if played straight.

lead_characters.name: Jessie
lead_characters.demographics: Female, early teens, gas station cashier.
lead_characters.hook: Jessie is the surprise wildcard who turns the gas-station sequence into a full-blown shootout. She starts as background texture and then detonates into one of the movie’s most memorable comic reversals.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a juicy scene-stealing role in the spirit of a young actor getting a breakout moment in a larger ensemble. The showcase is the sudden tonal flip from harmless cashier to armed chaos agent.

one older female role in the 80s range
one 30s female reporter with strong comic timing
one physically comedic male supporting role with inhaler use

technical.vfx_details: No meaningful VFX beyond basic blood/gunshot enhancement if desired.
technical.sfx_needs: Gunfire, blood squibs, body handling, vehicle impacts, practical trunk gag, and a few slapstick falls.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model; best suited to a streaming-first or specialty theatrical comedy rollout.

budget.note: Contemporary, mostly practical locations, no VFX load, and only modest stunt/squib work; the main cost drivers are company moves between the town, cottage, gas station, and warehouse.

casting.note: Tom and Stuart need a very specific comic chemistry, Karen needs authority with menace, and Electra has to play both vanity and competence; the child role and the 80s mother add a couple of narrower asks.

development.note: The premise is clear from page one and the escalation is easy to track; the main development conversation is tonal calibration, not story architecture.

comp_set.title: The Big White
comp_set.why_it_comps: Small-town crime comedy built around a body problem, escalating lies, and a lead who keeps trying to stay decent while the situation gets absurd.

comp_set.title: The Guard
comp_set.why_it_comps: A deadpan crime-comedy lane where local authority figures, criminal chaos, and sharp banter drive the engine.

comp_set.title: Fargo
comp_set.why_it_comps: The mix of regional specificity, escalating criminal incompetence, and darkly comic violence is the closest tonal cousin.

comp_set.title: The Death of Stalin
comp_set.why_it_comps: The script shares the pressure-cooker farce of public power colliding with private panic, even though the setting is much smaller and more contemporary.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who like crime comedies with escalating humiliation, small-town politics, and a lead who keeps making the wrong choice for understandable reasons.
audience_target.demographics: 25-54, slightly male-skewing but playable for couples and ensemble-comedy audiences; strongest with viewers who like broad, profane, high-concept farce.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary contained comedy with a handful of practical locations, a modest cast, and limited stunt/blood work.

types_of_buyers: specialty distributors looking for adult crowd-pleasers
lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane of adult, dialogue-driven crime farce with a strong central performance and a clean, easy-to-pitch premise. The town-wide election-day structure makes it feel commercial without requiring a large-scale production footprint.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature with a closed comic-crime arc; no clear sequel or spinoff vector beyond the core Tom/Stuart dynamic.

strengths.what_it_means: A buyer can understand the movie in one sentence, which is a real advantage in a crowded comedy market. That makes it easy to package around a director, a lead actor, or a streamer comedy slate looking for a clean hook.
strengths.evidence: The opening body-in-the-trunk setup and the election-day countdown are both clear within the first pages.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Tom is a strong comic lead role.
strengths.what_it_means: The movie has a center that can attract a name actor who wants to play panic, decency, and physical humiliation in the same performance. That kind of role is useful for buyers because it can be sold on casting as much as concept.
strengths.evidence: Tom’s superstition, his escalating attempts to hide the body, and his increasingly desperate public appearances.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The escalation is clean and relentless.
strengths.what_it_means: Each set piece creates a new problem instead of repeating the last one, which is exactly what keeps a comedy-thriller moving. That gives the script trailer-friendly momentum and a strong audience-retention profile.
strengths.evidence: Gas station panic, sheriff escort, live interview, house invasion, warehouse showdown, and the final fish-hook sting.

strengths.what_it_means: Tom/Stuart, Tom/Marilynn, Tom/Wendy, Karen/Freddie, and Tom/Electra all have playable friction, which gives the movie multiple comic engines. That helps both casting and marketing because the project isn’t dependent on one relationship alone.
strengths.evidence: The Justin household scenes, the newsroom banter, and the Karen/Freddie power dynamic all create distinct tonal pockets.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The small-town setting has usable texture.
strengths.what_it_means: The campaign posters, the local sheriff, the rental-car guy, the gas station, and the warehouse create a world that feels specific without becoming expensive. That’s a good fit for buyers who want a contained movie that still feels lived-in.
strengths.evidence: Chesterville’s election signage, local news coverage, and the repeated return to town institutions.

whats_special.headline: This is a clean, commercial contained comedy with a very easy hook: a mayoral candidate, a corpse, and one disastrous election day. It has the kind of lead role, ensemble chemistry, and practical production footprint that can attract a buyer without requiring a huge budget or heavy effects.

items.area: The humor is very broad and very specific.
items.detail: The script leans hard into profanity, farce, and repeated misunderstanding gags, which gives it energy but also narrows the buyer pool. That’s a real positioning question for theatrical comedy buyers who want either sharper satire or broader four-quadrant accessibility.

He spends much of the movie stalling, panicking, and improvising rather than driving the action, which works for comedy but limits the sense of agency. Buyers will weigh whether the lead’s passivity is part of the joke or a ceiling on the character’s long-term appeal.

items.area: The supporting cast is vivid but not deep.
items.detail: Karen, Freddie, Electra, Wendy, and Andy all pop quickly, but most of them function as strong comic types rather than layered people. That’s fine for a feature farce, but it means the movie is selling on execution and timing more than on hidden character depth.

items.area: The final-act mechanics get very busy.
items.detail: Once the house invasion, warehouse confrontation, live news coverage, and sheriff arrival all converge, the movie is juggling a lot of moving parts at once. The energy is high, but a producer will notice how much of the payoff depends on keeping every thread legible in the same stretch.

issues.headline: The main friction is tonal and market-facing rather than structural: this is a very funny, very profane crime farce that will play best to buyers who want broad adult comedy. The other watchout is that the movie’s supporting players are strong types more than deep characters, so the package lives or dies on the lead, the timing, and the execution of the set pieces.
